claims.claim: Film criticism is the study, interpretation, and evaluation of a film and its place in cinema history; it typically offers interpretation of meaning, analysis of structure and style, judgment of worth by comparison with other films, and an estimation of likely effect on viewers.

A movie review is consumer-oriented writing published around a film's release that emphasizes recommendation over analysis, usually explaining the premise and weighing a film's merits and flaws, often with a rating.

Film criticism is commonly divided into academic criticism (by film scholars, published in books and journals, rarely taking the form of a review) and journalistic criticism (in newspapers, magazines, and online outlets, mainly reviewing new releases).
Criticism can address several objects, including formal craft (cinematography, editing, sound, performance, design), narrative, representation, ideology, and audience effects.

Formalist criticism attends to how form and craft create meaning; it is associated with critics such as André Bazin and the Cahiers du Cinéma writers (including later directors François Truffaut and Jean-Luc Godard), and in later academic film studies with David Bordwell and Kristin Thompson.

Ideological criticism examines the values, assumptions, and power relations embedded in a work; such readings are contested, as with Birth of a Nation, praised by some critics for narrative complexity while others were outraged by its openly racist attitudes, and with strongly argued documentaries that some critics label propagandistic.
Feminist criticism, informed by feminist film theory, asks how a work represents gender and what assumptions about viewers it carries.

Audience-oriented criticism studies how viewers interpret and respond to media; early direct-effects assumptions that audiences passively accept media messages were challenged by research such as the 1940 People's Choice study, and scholars continue to disagree about how to study media effects.
Critics guide attention and can influence a film's early box-office performance, but critical reception and commercial success can diverge, and evaluation is argued rather than certified.

Professional journalism ethics, as codified by the Society of Professional Journalists, center on four principles — seek truth and report it, minimize harm, act independently, and be accountable — which imply for critics fairness, engaging the work, and disclosing conflicts of interest.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a critic's evaluation can be objective.
positions: Critics should deliver fair, evidence-based judgments, implying that objectivity is achievable and expected.
Evaluation is shaped by taste, values, and context; two critics can disagree about the same film without either lacking evidence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents evaluation as argued judgment supported by evidence, not as a certified verdict; disagreement is expected and does not by itself prove error.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether media produce direct effects on audiences.
positions: The early direct-effects model assumed passive audiences reacting predictably to media messages.
The 1940 People's Choice study and later research challenged that model; scholars disagree about whether and how media effects can be untangled.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats audience effects as a contested object of study and avoids asserting any specific effect of any specific work.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether ideological readings of a work describe the work itself or the critic's perspective.
positions: Some critics describe works as propagating values (for example, labeling strongly argued documentaries propagandistic).
Others treat such labels as contestable interpretations rather than established facts about the works.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes ideological claims as interpretations and marks contested labels as contested.

sourceRecords.provider: Saylor Academy (edition of the University of Minnesota Libraries open textbook)

Supports: critical reception and box-office success can diverge (films with a lousy critical reception can do extremely well when marketing creates enough hype); contested evaluation, e.g., Birth of a Nation praised by some critics for narrative complexity while others were outraged by its openly racist attitudes; American culture is not monolithic, with contingents opposing dominant ideologies; some critics labeling strongly argued documentaries propagandistic, reported as a contested question. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding Media and Culture: An Introduction to Mass Communication — Chapter 2: Media Effects
sourceRecords.provider: Saylor Academy (edition of the University of Minnesota Libraries open textbook)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live at the Saylor mirror on 2026-08-21. Supports: media messages can range from overt statements to vague expressions of cultural values; the direct-effects model of the 1920s and 1930s assumed audiences passively accepted media messages and reacted predictably; the 1940 People's Choice study challenged that model (undecided voters turned to family and community rather than media); scholars disagree about whether research can ever untangle the relationship of media and effects; studying possible media effects provides a crucial perspective on modern culture. Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Film criticism
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 and used as a reputable secondary overview (Tier D). Supports: film criticism as the analysis and evaluation of films and the film medium; the division into academic criticism (film scholars, books and journals, rarely review-shaped) and journalistic criticism (newspapers, magazines, online; mainly reviews of new releases that help readers decide whether to see a film, typically explaining the premise and discussing merits or flaws, often with ratings); named academic critics (André Bazin, Jean-Luc Godard, François Truffaut of Cahiers du Cinéma; Sergei Eisenstein; Kristin Thompson; David Bordwell); the early-20th-century emergence of film criticism and Canudo's 1911 'Seventh Art' manifesto; research findings that critics' judgments can influence a film's early box-office performance. Reference only; no wording reproduced.
